overview: This sensor (typified by the ML8511 breakout) uses a UV-sensitive photodiode to output an analog voltage that scales with ultraviolet intensity, covering both UVA and UVB wavelengths. Unlike a photoresistor, which responds to the full visible spectrum, this one is filtered to ignore visible and infrared light almost entirely — which matters because it means the sensor reads close to zero indoors under normal room lighting, even in a brightly lit office, since ordinary LED and fluorescent bulbs emit almost no UV. Meaningful readings require actual sunlight or a dedicated UV source, which trips up a lot of first-time testers who point it at a lamp and conclude the sensor is broken.
simpleSummary: A sensor that measures how strong the sun's UV rays are, reading near zero indoors under normal light bulbs.

specifications.outputType: Analog voltage, proportional to UV intensity
specifications.interface: Analog (requires an ADC input on the microcontroller)
specifications.outputVoltageRange: ~1V (low UV) up to ~2.8V (very strong midday sun), datasheet curve required to convert to a UV Index number
specifications.enablePin: EN pin for power-down mode when not sampling

pinMap.name: OUT
pinMap.function: Analog output voltage proportional to UV intensity; needs a conversion formula from the datasheet response curve to get an actual UV Index.
pinMap.gotcha: Reads near zero indoors under LED or fluorescent bulbs even in a brightly lit room, since those emit almost no UV — this is normal behavior, not a faulty sensor. Meaningful readings need actual sunlight.

pinMap.name: EN
pinMap.function: Enable pin — pull HIGH to power the sensor, LOW to shut it down and save current.
pinMap.gotcha: Left floating on some breakouts rather than defaulting HIGH — if readings are always zero, check this pin is actually pulled HIGH before assuming the sensor itself is bad.

pinMap.name: 3V3
pinMap.function: Regulated 3.3V reference output on most breakouts, useful as a stable ADC reference voltage.

useCases.title: Wearable sunburn-risk alert
useCases.scenario: A wrist-worn or clip-on device buzzes or lights up once cumulative UV exposure crosses a threshold for the wearer's skin type.

useCases.title: Weather station UV Index add-on
useCases.scenario: Add real-time UV Index alongside temperature/humidity/pressure readings on a home weather station dashboard.

useCases.title: Greenhouse UV monitoring
useCases.scenario: Track natural UV levels reaching plants through a greenhouse roof to decide whether supplemental grow lighting is needed.

useCases.title: Outdoor UV safety sign
useCases.scenario: Drive a public-facing display (e.g. at a pool or park) that shows the current UV Index and a plain-language risk level.

commonlyPairedWith: BME280 (for a full outdoor weather station)
oftenConfusedWith: LDR/photoresistor (measures visible light brightness, not UV)
IR flame/proximity sensors (opposite end of the spectrum, unrelated)
oftenUpgradedTo: VEML6075 / LTR-390 (digital I2C UV sensors with factory-calibrated UV Index output, no analog conversion math needed)

beginnerMistakes: Testing indoors under a lamp and concluding the sensor is dead — ordinary indoor lighting emits almost no UV, so a near-zero reading indoors is expected, not a fault.
Testing through a closed window — ordinary glass blocks most UVB, so readings taken behind glass read much lower than the true outdoor UV Index.
Treating the raw output voltage as the UV Index directly instead of applying the datasheet's linear conversion formula (which includes a zero-intensity offset voltage).
Touching or scratching the sensing element's surface — the exposed UV-transmissive window is more delicate than an ordinary plastic sensor cover.
Comparing readings taken at different times of day without accounting for the sun's angle — UV intensity swings dramatically between morning and solar noon even with clear skies.
